issues.legal_issue: Admissions made by family members to obtain an advantage are not decisive evidence of separation from a joint family.
material_facts: Family members made inconsistent statements about whether the family had separated in different proceedings and circumstances.
The court found that the statements had been made to meet particular contingencies or obtain advantages.
Other evidence showed the family members’ continuing relations with the family estate and joint affairs.
issues.conclusion: The admissions were of little value in determining whether the family members had separated; their relations with the estate were more significant.
issues.legal_principle: As stated in Alluri Venkatapathi Raju v. Dantuluri Venkatanarasimha Raju, statements may serve a person’s purpose or proceed from ignorance of the true position. The question of separation should be determined by considering the members’ relations with the estate, not merely their statements.

predicates.joint_family_separation_dispute: The dispute concerns whether members of a family that was claimed to be joint had separated.
predicates.family_members_made_admissions_to_gain_a: Family members made statements about separation to meet particular circumstances or obtain an advantage.

issues.definition: When a separation dispute involves family members’ advantage-seeking admissions, those admissions are not decisive evidence of separation.

issues.legal_issue: An objection that a plaintiff omitted further relief from a declaratory suit should not be raised for the first time on appeal when it could have been raised earlier and the plaintiff could then have amended the claim.
material_facts: The suit sought a declaration without further relief.
The objection that further relief should have been sought was not pleaded or raised at trial.
The objection was raised for the first time in the High Court, where the suggested further relief was partition.
If the objection had been raised earlier, the plaintiff could have sought an amendment to the claim.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to allow the objection to be raised at that late stage and did not decide whether further relief was required.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, concerns a plaintiff who can seek further relief but omits to do so. The court applied the settled practice of allowing a plaintiff to amend rather than automatically dismissing a suit, and held that the objection should have been raised at the earliest stage so that amendment could be sought.

predicates.appeal_in_declaratory_suit: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking declaratory relief.
predicates.further_relief_objection_not_raised_at_t: The opposing party did not raise at trial the objection that the plaintiff should have sought further relief.
predicates.plaintiff_could_seek_amendment_if_object: The plaintiff could have asked to amend the claim if the objection had been raised at an earlier stage.

issues.definition: In an appeal in a declaratory suit, a further-relief objection left unraised at trial is not entertained when the plaintiff could have sought an amendment if given the objection earlier.

issues.legal_issue: A new limitation plea may be considered on appeal when allowing it causes no prejudice because no additional facts could have been proved to meet it.
material_facts: The limitation plea was first raised in the High Court.
The respondent argued that the plea should not be allowed because it had not been raised earlier.
When asked what further facts could have been proved had the plea been raised earlier, counsel could not identify any.
issues.conclusion: The court allowed the limitation plea to be considered on appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The court distinguished a new plea that could prejudice the opposing party from one that would not require further evidence. Because the respondent could not have put forward additional facts to meet the limitation plea, the court saw no reason to reject it at that stage.

predicates.appeal_in_civil_suit: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil suit.
predicates.limitation_plea_raised_late: A party first raised the limitation plea at an appellate stage.
predicates.opposing_party_could_not_prove_additiona: The opposing party could identify no additional facts it could have proved if the limitation plea had been raised earlier.

issues.definition: A late limitation plea may be considered in a civil appeal when the opposing party could not have proved additional facts to meet it.

issues.legal_issue: For a declaratory suit governed by the residual limitation rule, the right to sue accrues when the defendant effectively threatens the asserted right, not upon an earlier event that does not invade or jeopardize it.
material_facts: The trust document was executed and the house was built while the family was using the arrangements for its benefit.
The claimant’s father lived in the house, and the claimant later lived there as well.
The claimant knew of litigation concerning the property but was not a party to it, and its decree did not bind him or affect his possession.
The claimant objected when a court-appointed commissioner came to measure the house to carry out a partition, and the claimant filed suit within six years of that event.
issues.conclusion: The claimant’s right to sue accrued when the commissioner’s visit effectively threatened his asserted right, and the suit was within time.
issues.legal_principle: Article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, provides a six-year period running from when the right to sue accrues. Under Bolo v. Koklan, Annamalai Chettiar v. A.M.K.C.T. Muthukaruppan Chettiar, and Govinda Narayan Singh v. Sham Lal Singh, a right to sue accrues upon infringement or a clear and unequivocal threat of infringement. As explained in Pothukutchi Appa Rao v. Secretary of State, a denial without an effective invasion or jeopardy does not necessarily compel a declaratory suit.

predicates.declaratory_suit_under_residual_limitati: The proceeding is a declaratory suit for which no specific limitation period is provided elsewhere.
predicates.earlier_events_did_not_effectively_threa: Earlier documents, conduct, or litigation did not effectively invade or jeopardize the claimant’s asserted right.
predicates.later_event_effectively_threatened_asser: A later event clearly and effectively threatened the claimant’s asserted right.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_period_afte: The claimant filed suit within the applicable limitation period after the effective threat.

issues.definition: A declaratory suit is not time-barred when earlier events did not effectively threaten the asserted right, a later event did, and the suit was filed within the limitation period after that threat.

issues.legal_issue: Property acquired with the aid of a sufficient joint-family nucleus is joint-family property unless the person asserting separate ownership proves that it was acquired without that aid.
material_facts: The family continued to be joint and carried on business together despite documents purporting to record separation.
The court found that the relinquishment documents and trust deed were colourable parts of a scheme to protect family assets from creditors.
The family had extensive property and business income sufficient to provide the funds used for the trust and construction of the house.
No reliable evidence established that the person who executed the trust had separate income sufficient to fund the trust and the house.
Other family members supervised construction, paid contractors, and obtained receipts; the trustees were connected with the family, and the trust was brought to an end.
issues.conclusion: The trust deed was colourable and fictitious, the property was joint-family property, and the respondent was entitled to the declaration sought.
issues.legal_principle: Hindu law presumes a family to be joint, but does not presume that property held by a family member is joint-family property. The person asserting that property is joint-family property bears the initial burden; proof of a sufficient family nucleus from which the property could have been acquired shifts the burden to the person asserting separate ownership to show acquisition without the family’s assistance. A document purporting to effect separation may be shown to be sham and not intended to be acted upon. The court also relied on Alluri Venkatapathi Raju v. Dantuluri Venkatanarasimha Raju when assessing admissions of separation.

rule.if: suit_to_declare_trust_document_sham and family_remained_joint and sufficient_joint_family_nucleus_existed and claimant_failed_to_prove_acquisition_from_separate_funds and transaction_fitted_family_asset_protection_scheme

predicates.suit_to_declare_trust_document_sham: The proceeding seeks a declaration that a trust document is sham and does not affect the claimant’s rights in the property.
predicates.family_remained_joint: The family members continued to conduct joint affairs and remained connected with the family estate despite documents asserting separation.
predicates.sufficient_joint_family_nucleus_existed: The family had property or income sufficient to provide the funds from which the disputed property could have been acquired.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_acquisition_fro: The person asserting separate ownership did not reliably establish that the property was acquired without assistance from family property or funds.
predicates.transaction_fitted_family_asset_protecti: The trust and related documents formed part of arrangements used to protect family assets from creditors.

issues.definition: When a sham-trust challenge concerns property acquired while the family remained joint, a sufficient family nucleus existed, separate funding was not proved, and the transaction fitted an asset-protection scheme, the property is joint-family property and the trust does not defeat the claimant’s rights.
